To calculate compound interest in Excel or Google Sheets, use =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for a lump sum balance or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) when adding regular contributions. Tools for this journey Compound interest calculator → Retirement spreadsheet template guide → How savings account interest is calculated → On This Page How to Calculate Compound Interest in Excel and Google Sheets The Compound Interest Formula Step by Step Adding Monthly Contributions With FV Daily, Monthly and Yearly Compounding Compared Common Spreadsheet Mistakes Our Takeaway How to Calculate Compound Interest in Excel and Google Sheets To calculate compound interest in a spreadsheet, enter =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for an initial lump sum or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) for recurring contributions. In these formulas, P represents initial principal, r is the annual interest rate, n is compounding periods per year, and t is total investment years. In our internal modeling, we ran both formulas on a $10,000 initial balance at a 5% nominal rate over 10 years, confirming that monthly compounding produces a future value (FV) of $16,470.09. We verified our mathematical power outputs against a month-by-month calculation loop and checked the built-in function against the documented test case published by Microsoft Support , which confirms =FV(0.06/12,10,-200,-500,1) equals $2,581.40. Spreadsheets require cash outflows to be entered as negative numbers. If you omit the negative signs before regular contributions or initial principal, the formula produces a negative future balance. When regular deposits occur on a different timeline than compounding, such as monthly deposits alongside daily compounding, you must compute an effective periodic rate rather than using a simple rate division. The Compound Interest Formula Step by Step The standard compound interest formula evaluates exponential asset growth using the equation A = P*(1 + r/n)^(n*t). Each component represents a concrete variable in your savings plan: A is the final future balance after all interest accrues. P is the starting principal balance. r is the nominal annual interest rate expressed as a decimal. n is the number of times interest compounds per calendar year. t is the overall duration of the investment in years. Consider a starting balance of $10,000 invested at 5% nominal annual interest for 10 years with monthly compounding. In cell format, write =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10). The term 0.05/12 divides the annual percentage rate (APR) into a monthly rate of approximately 0.004167, while 12*10 calculates the 120 total compounding periods. Evaluating this expression yields $16,470.09. Changing the compounding frequency alters the exponent and periodic divisor. Using the same $10,000 balance at 5% over 10 years, annual compounding (n=1) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/1)^(1*10) produces $16,288.95. Quarterly compounding (n=4) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) yields $16,436.19. Daily compounding (n=365) entered as =10000*(1+0.05/365)^(365*10) grows to $16,486.65. You can also evaluate a lump sum using the built-in future value syntax =FV(0.05/12,12*10,0,-10000), which returns the identical $16,470.09. Adding Monthly Contributions With FV When you add recurring savings to an existing investment, use the future value function documented on the Microsoft Support and Google Docs Editors Help pages. Both platforms implement the syntax FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]). The arguments represent specific cash flow parameters: rate is the interest rate applied per single period. nper is the total count of compounding payment periods. pmt is the cash deposit added each period. pv is the present value or initial principal balance. type indicates payment timing, where 0 represents the end of the period and 1 represents the beginning. For a $10,000 starting balance with $200 deposited at the end of each month at 5% annual interest for 10 years, enter =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200,-10000). This returns $47,526.55. Over 10 years, your cumulative cash contributions total $34,000, consisting of the $10,000 principal plus $24,000 in monthly additions. Total compound interest earned equals $13,526.55. If you initiate deposits at the beginning of each period instead, enter =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200,-10000,1), which yields $47,655.95. If you begin with zero initial principal and contribute only regular monthly deposits, omit the principal entry: =FV(0.05/12,12*10,-200) yields $31,056.46. When deposits and compounding occur strictly once per year, enter =FV(5%,10,-2400,-10000), returning $46,475.89. One condition applies: the basic =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) shortcut assumes the contribution schedule matches the compounding frequency. If you contribute $200 monthly while the financial institution compounds interest daily, standard rate division slightly understates growth. To resolve this mismatch, calculate the effective monthly rate using (1+0.05/365)^(365/12)-1, which equals about 0.0041750727. Entering =FV(0.0041750727,12*10,-200,-10000) produces about $47,559.87. That creates a difference of about $33 over 10 years compared to the simple monthly division output of $47,526.55. Daily, Monthly and Yearly Compounding Compared Increasing the frequency of compounding periods accelerates overall account growth by adding accrued interest to the principal base earlier. To see how deposit institutions handle these daily mechanics, read our review of how savings account interest is calculated . The table below models a $10,000 principal deposit earning a 5% nominal annual interest rate over a 10-year term across different compounding frequencies: Compounding Frequency Periodic Divisor (n) Formula Syntax Future Value (10 Years) Effective Annual Percentage Yield (APY) Annually 1 =10000*(1+0.05/1)^(1*10) $16,288.95 5.0000% Quarterly 4 =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) $16,436.19 5.0945% Monthly 12 =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10) $16,470.09 5.1162% Daily 365 =10000*(1+0.05/365)^(365*10) $16,486.65 5.1267% Daily compounding produces $197.70 more in accumulated interest than annual compounding on a $10,000 balance over 10 years. For continuous compounding benchmarks, theoretical growth reaches $16,487.21 under identical terms. Annual percentage yield (APY) measures this true annualized return. A 5% nominal annual rate yields an effective 5.1162% under monthly compounding and 5.1267% under daily compounding. Common Spreadsheet Mistakes Formulas fail when users mismatch timing inputs or violate spreadsheet sign rules. Avoid these three common calculation errors: Entering annual interest rates against monthly periods. Passing an unadjusted annual rate such as 5% or 0.05 alongside 120 monthly periods in =FV(0.05, 120, -200, -10000) causes the software to apply a 5% return each individual month. This mistake inflates the projected balance to $4,880,767.80 instead of the true $47,526.55 balance. Always divide the annual rate by your annual periods. Omitting negative signs on outgoing deposits and principal. Microsoft Support documents the sign convention for these functions. Money deposited represents cash leaving your hand, which must be entered as a negative number. Writing =FV(0.05/12, 120, 200, 10000) yields -$47,526.55. Insert negative signs before payment and present value arguments to display positive savings balances. Ignoring compounding and contribution schedule mismatches. The standard FV formula assumes periodic contributions occur on the identical schedule as interest compounding. If you deposit funds monthly but earn interest compounded daily, using naive monthly division understates growth. Converting your nominal daily rate into an effective monthly rate eliminates this variance. Our Takeaway To model investment compounding accurately, use =FV(rate/n, n*years, -deposit, -principal) whenever your deposit frequency matches your compounding schedule, or =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for fixed lump-sum balances. This spreadsheet modeling approach is not suitable for individuals seeking instant figures without formula entry, nor does it accommodate variable-rate products. Readers requiring fast comparisons across custom scenarios can model their numbers using our compound interest calculator . Our recommendation would change if deposit accounts adjust to floating rates, if tax withholding or custodial platform fees are subtracted from annual growth, or if a spreadsheet platform changes how its FV function takes arguments. For your next step, copy our verified formulas into your personal workbook to audit your current wealth accumulation schedule. Frequently Asked Questions How to calculate compound interest in Excel? Calculate compound interest in Excel using =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) for a lump sum or =FV(rate/n, n*years, -pmt, -pv) for recurring payments. For example, a $10,000 lump sum at 5% interest for 10 years compounded monthly is entered as =10000*(1+0.05/12)^(12*10), which outputs $16,470.09. Enter outgoing investments as negative numbers to ensure the function outputs a positive balance. Is compound interest calculated monthly or yearly? Compound interest can compound on any schedule specified by the financial institution, commonly daily, monthly, or yearly. On a $10,000 balance at 5% over 10 years, annual compounding produces $16,288.95 while monthly compounding produces $16,470.09. Does the same compound interest formula work in Google Sheets? Yes, Google Sheets uses the same syntax and argument order as Excel for calculating compound interest. Both applications accept the standard mathematical power equation =P*(1+r/n)^(n*t) as well as the built-in financial function =FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]). How do you calculate quarterly or half-yearly compounding? Calculate quarterly compounding by setting the periodic divisor n to 4, and half-yearly compounding by setting n to 2. For a $10,000 investment at 5% for 10 years compounded quarterly, the formula =10000*(1+0.05/4)^(4*10) produces $16,436.19. To model semi-annual compounding under the same parameters, replace the divisor and multiplier with 2 in the formula =P*(1+r/2)^(2*t). How do you include monthly deposits in the compound interest formula? Include monthly deposits by using the future value function =FV(rate/12, 12*years, -monthly_deposit, -initial_principal). For a $10,000 starting balance with $200 added at the end of each month at 5% interest over 10 years, enter =FV(0.05/12, 12*10, -200, -10000). This returns $47,526.55, reflecting $34,000 in total out-of-pocket deposits and $13,526.55 in earned compound interest. What interest rate should you enter in spreadsheet formulas? Enter the periodic interest rate, which is the nominal annual rate divided by the number of compounding periods per year. If your annual rate is 5% and interest compounds monthly, enter 0.05/12 or 5%/12 as the rate argument. Entering the full annual rate of 0.05 alongside 120 monthly periods erroneously calculates 5% growth per month, severely overstating results. When sizing residential debt, always verify your specific county tax rate to avoid sudden shifts in debt-to-income underwriting. Property tax adds roughly (effective rate x home price) / 12 to your monthly principal and interest payment, ranging from about $97 a month in Hawaii to about $627 a month in New Jersey and Illinois on a $400,000 home. Evaluating the tax baseline in your target region helps protect against unexpected escrow shortages after closing. The breakdown below details the monthly property tax impact across all 50 states using standardized baseline pricing. Tools for this journey PITI Mortgage Calculator → Mortgage Affordability Calculator → Hidden Cost of Owning a Home Calculator → On This Page Property Tax Added to a $400,000 Mortgage by State How the Estimate Works Highest and Lowest Property Tax States What Else Goes Into Escrow Our Takeaway Property Tax Added to a $400,000 Mortgage by State Property tax adds about (effective rate x home price) / 12 a month to a borrower's housing expense, which translates to about $97 in Hawaii up to about $627 in New Jersey and Illinois on a $400,000 home. The District of Columbia carries an effective property tax rate of 0.60%, which adds $200 a month on a $400,000 residence and sits outside the 50-state ranking. Across the entire country, the median state effective rate results in a monthly property tax charge of about $263. How the Estimate Works To calculate the monthly tax portion of a mortgage payment, multiply your home purchase price by the state effective rate and divide the total by 12. In our internal modeling, we converted each state's effective rate to a monthly dollar figure on a $400,000 home using baseline data from the Tax Foundation . The underlying data comes from the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) of the U.S. Census Bureau . An effective property tax rate represents the percentage of total owner-occupied market value paid in taxes. State averages often conceal dramatic county-level variations. In New Jersey, for example, county-level effective rates span from 0.93% in Cape May County to 2.47% in Camden County. That means an identical $400,000 purchase incurs about $310 a month in property taxes in Cape May County, but about $823 a month in Camden County. A buyer relying solely on the New Jersey state average of $627 a month faces a substantial discrepancy when closing on a home in either jurisdiction. Highest and Lowest Property Tax States The five states with the highest monthly property taxes on a $400,000 home are New Jersey ($627), Illinois ($627), Connecticut ($513), Vermont ($503), and New Hampshire ($500). A higher monthly tax leaves less of your budget for the loan payment. You can test how a higher or lower tax changes what you can afford with our mortgage affordability calculator . Conversely, the five lowest property tax states for owner-occupied housing are Hawaii ($97 at 0.29%), Alabama ($123 at 0.37%), Utah ($160 at 0.48%), Arizona ($160 at 0.48%), and South Carolina ($163 at 0.49%). What Else Goes Into Escrow Property tax is only one piece of a mortgage payment. Our state comparison table models property taxes alone, meaning homeowners insurance premiums and private mortgage insurance remain excluded from these specific figures. Homeowners association (HOA) dues are also not included. To calculate your comprehensive monthly housing obligation including all loan and insurance components, utilize our PITI mortgage calculator , where PITI stands for principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. If you know your county's effective rate, use it in the same formula instead of the state figure. Our guide to mortgage mistakes before applying covers other costs buyers overlook. Our Takeaway Property tax can add from about $97 to about $627 a month on a $400,000 home depending on state, and your county rate decides the real number. This benchmark modeling applies to owner-occupied residential properties assessed at the exact $400,000 baseline price. This analysis is not applicable to residential tenants, who pay shelter expenses via lease agreements rather than direct tax bills, nor does it capture multi-million-dollar purchases without linear adjustment. If your home purchase differs from $400,000, scale the monthly dollar figures proportionally by multiplying the state rate against your target valuation before dividing by 12. Our conclusions would change if local taxing jurisdictions revise their assessment ratios, if state legislatures expand homestead exemption limits, or if the Tax Foundation publishes updated effective rates. Multiply your own price by your county's effective rate and divide by 12 before you make an offer. Frequently Asked Questions Does a mortgage calculator include property tax and insurance? Some mortgage calculators cover only principal and interest, while others add property tax and insurance. To compute your complete monthly housing expense including tax and insurance escrows, enter your loan and property details into our PITI mortgage calculator . How much is property tax on a $400,000 house in the highest and lowest states? On a $400,000 home, property taxes add about $627 a month in New Jersey and Illinois at the top of the state rankings, compared to about $97 a month in Hawaii at the bottom. The median state level sits at roughly $263 a month. What is an effective property tax rate? An effective property tax rate measures the annual property tax paid as a percentage of the total market value of owner-occupied housing. It lets you compare states on one scale. Why do property taxes differ inside the same state? Rates differ by county inside a state. For instance, New Jersey county rates span from 0.93% in Cape May County to 2.47% in Camden County, creating very different monthly payments on identical home prices. Is homeowners insurance included in the monthly property tax figures? Homeowners insurance is not included in the monthly property tax figures on this page. How do I calculate monthly property taxes for my specific home price? To calculate monthly property taxes for your specific home price, multiply your target purchase price by your local effective tax rate percentage and divide the resulting figure by 12. acceptedAnswer.text: Rates differ by county inside a state. For instance, New Jersey county rates span from 0.93% in Cape May County to 2.47% in Camden County, creating very different monthly payments on identical home prices.

mainEntity.name: Is homeowners insurance included in the monthly property tax figures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Homeowners insurance is not included in the monthly property tax figures on this page.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate monthly property taxes for my specific home price?

acceptedAnswer.text: To calculate monthly property taxes for your specific home price, multiply your target purchase price by your local effective tax rate percentage and divide the resulting figure by 12.

semantic.text: ModernWallet Free Financial Calculators Calculators All calculators Auto Loan Mortgage Retirement Investing Portfolio Real Estate Net Worth Budget Tax Resolution Estate Planning Probate Elder Care Trump Account 529 College Savings Coast FIRE Business Loan Payoff Personal Loan Interest Per Day Taxable vs. Tax-Deferred Credit Card Payoff IUL Merchant Cash Advance Invoice Factoring Business Line of Credit PTO Cash-Out Zakat Life Insurance Needs Self-Employment Tax Operating Cash Flow Mileage Deduction Cash Conversion Cycle Freelance Rate HELOC S-Corp Tax Commercial Mortgage CD Calculator Emergency Fund Debt Consolidation Inflation Expense Ratio Social Security Break-Even Mileage Reimbursement Portfolio Rebalancing Hurricane Deductible Annuity Credit Card Interest Loan Payment HYSA vs CD Trump Account vs 529 Mortgage Recast Social Security COLA Biweekly Mortgage Roth vs Traditional 401(k) Pay Off Mortgage or Invest Florida Amendment 3 Student Loan Garnishment Tax Bracket Debt-to-Income Ratio Taxable Social Security Checklists Charitable Donation Deduction Salary Car Loan Interest Deduction Paycheck Rent vs Buy Rule of 78 Stock Capital Gains Tax Debt Payoff Hidden Cost of Owning a Home × ModernWallet / Mortgage / Mortgage Calculator With Taxes And Insurance PITI Mortgage Calculator By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated November 25, 2026 · How we review PITI stands for Principal, Interest, Taxes, and Insurance, the four components of your true all-in monthly mortgage payment. The calculator above shows your principal and interest (P&I). Add your estimated property taxes and homeowner's insurance below to calculate your full PITI. Why does this matter? When applying the 28% front-end debt-to-income (DTI) rule, lenders use your PITI, not just P&I. That means your PITI must remain below 28% of your gross monthly income to qualify for most conventional loans. $2,076 monthly payment $427,185 total interest 30 years to payoff Share Interactive — edit any field How it's calculated PITI is calculated by adding four line items: principal and interest from your amortization schedule, monthly property taxes (annual tax ÷ 12), monthly homeowner's insurance (annual premium ÷ 12), and PMI if your down payment is less than 20%. The calculator above handles the P&I portion; the remaining components depend on your location and loan structure. Property taxes vary widely by state and county. State effective rates in the Tax Foundation 2026 table run from 0.29% in Hawaii to 1.88% in New Jersey and Illinois, with a typical state near 0.8%, measured against home market value. See property tax by state for the monthly figure in each state on a $400,000 home. Private mortgage insurance (PMI) typically runs 0.5–1.5% of the loan amount annually for borrowers with less than 20% down, according to the CFPB. PMI is split into 12 monthly installments. Once your equity reaches 20%, you can request PMI cancellation under the Homeowners Protection Act; at 22% equity it is automatically terminated. A worked example Say you buy a $400,000 home with 20% down ($80,000), leaving a $320,000 loan at 6.75% for 30 years. P&I works out to $2,075.68 per month. Property taxes at an assumed 1.1% of home value on $400,000 add $366.67 per month. Homeowner's insurance at a typical $1,500 per year adds $125 per month. Because you put 20% down, there is no PMI. Total PITI: $2,567.35 per month. To qualify conventionally under the 28% front-end rule, you would need at least $9,169 per month in gross income ($2,567.35 ÷ 0.28). Common mistakes to avoid Budgeting only for principal and interest. Taxes and insurance together often add $300–$600 or more per month on a median-priced home, which can push PITI above the lender's 28% front-end limit. Forgetting PMI when putting less than 20% down. On a $350,000 loan at 1% annual PMI, that adds $292 per month — a cost that disappears once you reach 20% equity. Using the list-price assessed value to estimate taxes. Assessed value can differ significantly from market price depending on your county. Ask the listing agent for the seller's current tax bill. Ignoring homeowner's insurance cost differences by location. Coastal or flood-prone areas can carry premiums three to four times the national average. Get a quote before finalizing your budget. Not asking about escrow. Most lenders escrow taxes and insurance, collecting them monthly as part of your payment. If yours does not, you must budget to pay those bills yourself at year-end. Frequently asked questions What does PITI stand for in a mortgage? PITI stands for Principal, Interest, Taxes, and Insurance. These four items make up your total monthly housing cost. Lenders use your full PITI payment — not just principal and interest — when calculating your front-end debt-to-income ratio. What is the 28% rule for PITI? The 28% rule says your PITI should not exceed 28% of your gross monthly income. This is the conventional front-end DTI limit used by most lenders. For example, if you earn $8,000 per month before taxes, your PITI should stay at or below $2,240. How much is PMI and when can I remove it? PMI typically costs 0.5–1.5% of your loan amount per year, according to the CFPB. You can request cancellation once your equity reaches 20% of the original purchase price. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, your lender must automatically cancel PMI when your loan balance reaches 78% of the original value. How do I estimate property taxes for my PITI? Divide the annual property tax bill by 12. If you do not have the actual tax bill, use the county's current millage rate applied to the assessed value. State effective rates in the Tax Foundation 2026 table run from 0.29% in Hawaii to 1.88% in New Jersey and Illinois, with a typical state near 0.8%, and local rates vary significantly. Is homeowner's insurance required for a mortgage? Yes. Nearly all lenders require homeowner's insurance for the life of the loan. The premium varies by location, home value, coverage level, and risk factors like flood zone or fire risk. Your lender will typically collect it monthly through your escrow account. Does a mortgage calculator include closing costs and escrow? A basic principal-and-interest calculator does not include closing costs or escrow — that's exactly why PITI exists as a separate figure. Closing costs (2–5% of the loan amount, per the CFPB) are a one-time cash need at signing, while escrow collects your recurring property tax and insurance payments monthly as part of PITI. Use the calculator above for P&I, then add taxes and insurance from the sections above to see your full monthly cost. Does checking a mortgage calculator affect my credit score? No. Running numbers through a mortgage calculator, including this one, does not pull your credit report or affect your score in any way — it's a math tool, not a loan application. Your score is only affected once a lender runs a hard credit inquiry as part of an actual preapproval or application. Does PITI vary by state? Yes. The T and the I in PITI move with your state and county. The P&I portion does not. Per the Tax Foundation, state effective property tax rates run from 0.29% of home value in Hawaii to 1.88% in New Jersey and Illinois, with a typical state near 0.8%. Insurance adds another layer of variation. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) found inflation-adjusted premiums rising 18.3% to 43.3% across U.S. regions between 2018 and 2024 in its own market analysis. Pull your county's actual tax bill and a real insurance quote before you trust any PITI estimate for your target home.
